title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. For completeness, a parameterized language is a set of pairs \((x,k)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\), with both components explicitly encoded. It belongs to FPT if one uniform deterministic machine decides it within \(h(k)(M+2)^a\) steps for a total computable positive h, a fixed nonnegative integer a and complete encoding length M. A parameterized many-one reduction computes a single output pair \((y,k^{\prime})\) in such a time bound, preserves yes versus no membership, and satisfies \(k^{\prime}\le g(k)\) for a total computable function g; writing the output counts toward its runtime. The class W[1] can equivalently be defined as all parameterized languages admitting such a reduction to the Clique problem just specified. This characterization fixes the reduction convention without a change of target. It includes FPT, and Clique belongs to it, so FPT membership of Clique is equivalent to equality of the two classes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: The textbook specifies parameterized reductions and proves the completeness framework for Clique, via its complement relation with Independent Set. Theorem 14.21 derives the stronger exclusion of \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) Clique algorithms assuming ETH.

Bottesch identifies the FPT-versus-W[1] separation as the central conjecture, explains its known implications relative to P versus NP and ETH, and proves structural results with explicitly specified oracle conventions. These do not prove the unrelativized separation.
Lin gives a gap reduction showing that a constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique would imply an exact FPT algorithm. The consequence remains conditional on FPT differing from W[1].

Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit and Liu give a combinatorial proof of the \(k^{o(1)}\) parameterized inapproximability consequence under W[1]-hardness. The checked August 2024 revision precedes the SOSA 2025 publication.

Abboud, Fischer and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique bounds by logarithmic factors. Their August 2024 author revision retains a polynomial exponent depending on k; the institutional record lists the Algorithmica publication on 22 May 2026.

status_note: The textbook and Bottesch explicitly state the unresolved separation, and the later approximation papers retain it as an assumption. The checked fixed-k algorithm paper and its 2026 publication metadata provide no FPT algorithm. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; the review does not independently reprove the cited results.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

sentences: A k-clique is a set of k graph vertices joined by every possible edge.
The question asks for one exact deterministic algorithm whose input-size exponent is constant while a computable multiplier absorbs all dependence on k.
Polynomial time separately for each fixed k does not establish that uniform bound.
Clique completeness makes the question equivalent to FPT equalling W[1].
Conditional lower bounds and recent fixed-k or approximation results explain the conjecture’s significance without deciding it.
